body:
## Most office moves go wrong twelve months before anyone starts packing

The boxes are the easy part. Any removalist can move a floor of desks over a weekend.

What goes wrong in an office relocation is almost always a date. A notice period that passed. A make good clause nobody read. A fibre connection ordered six weeks before move day when it needed twelve. Furniture ordered after the builder finished instead of before.

None of those are hard problems. They're just problems that had to be solved earlier than they felt urgent.

This is the order to do it in.

## 12+ months out — before you decide anything

**Read your lease. Properly.**

Three things in it will shape everything that follows:

- **Your expiry date and any option to renew.** Options have notice windows. Miss the window and the option is usually gone, which hands your landlord the negotiating position.
- **The notice period for exercising or declining.** Often six months. Sometimes twelve. This is the single most common thing businesses find out too late.
- **Your make good obligations.** What condition you're contractually required to return the space in. This can run to tens of thousands of dollars and it is rarely budgeted for.

**Get a realistic headcount forecast.** Not today's number. The number in year three of the next lease. Most businesses either sign for the team they have and outgrow it, or sign for a growth plan that doesn't happen and pay rent on empty desks for five years.

**Decide whether you're moving, renewing or buying.** All three are live options. Staying can be the right answer, and knowing what the market would give you elsewhere is what makes a renewal negotiation work.

## 9–12 months out — brief and budget

- Write a brief: size, location, parking, meeting rooms, must-haves versus nice-to-haves
- Set a total project budget — rent, fit out, [furniture](/furniture), IT, moving, make good on the old space
- Decide who owns this internally. One person. If it's shared between three people it belongs to nobody
- Engage a [tenant representative](/tenant-rep) if you want someone on your side of the table. Worth knowing: commercial agents work for the landlord, not for you. Most business owners don't know this
- Start looking at what's actually available, including off-market. More than half of commercial property here transacts before it appears on a listing site

**A note on budget:** think of it as a pie. From the day the project starts, a long list of contractors, suppliers and agents all need a slice. The ones at the front take theirs early. If nobody is protecting the budget, quality drops at the back end — which is always furniture, IT and finishes, the parts your staff actually touch.

## 6–9 months out — find it and negotiate it

- Inspect the shortlist. Take photos of the ceiling, the risers and the loading dock, not just the view
- Check the lease terms carefully before you sign the next one — the same mistakes don't have to repeat
- Get your [tenant representative](/tenant-rep) negotiating before you fall in love with a space
- Brief your builders, designers and project managers so they're ready to move when you find the right place
- Confirm the make good scope on the outgoing space — get trades quotes early. This is not a month-before job
- Order [furniture](/furniture) and [desks](/blog/height-adjustable-desks-newcastle) as soon as the floor plan is settled — 4–8 weeks from order to install for stocked commercial ranges
- Check the building's fit out rules, after-hours access and dock booking process before you fall in love with it
- Ask what incentives are on the table. Rent-free periods, fit out contributions, reduced make good, cash contributions. These exist in almost every deal and most tenants never see them
- Get a written offer with the incentives in it
- Confirm the outgoings, not just the face rent. Face rent and net effective rent are different numbers

Newcastle specifics worth checking: Honeysuckle buildings usually have proper dock access and booking systems. Older Hunter Street and Newcastle East stock often has one small lift and street loading only, which changes your fit out program and your move day. Heritage buildings can restrict what you're allowed to fix to a wall.

## 4–6 months out — lease, design and approvals

- Have a solicitor review the lease. Every time. The cost of the review is trivial against the cost of a clause you didn't understand
- Confirm the fit out design against the final floor plan
- Lodge any approvals required — building, fire, and council for signage
- Appoint your fit out contractor, or someone to manage them on your behalf
- Confirm the landlord's fit out approval process. Most require plans signed off before a tool comes out
- Order your IT and comms now. A new business fibre service can take months, not weeks. Confirm the lead time with your provider in writing and ask specifically whether the building already has a lead-in

## 3–4 months out — order the long-lead items

- Order [furniture](/furniture). Allow 4–8 weeks for stocked commercial ranges, longer for custom joinery or made-to-order finishes. Furniture ordered after the builder finishes is why staff spend three weeks working from home after a move
- Confirm desk positions against the electrical and data layout. Moving a floor box after the slab work is expensive
- Order signage — external signage often needs council approval and lead time
- Book the removalist. Good ones book out, especially at end of quarter and end of financial year
- Start the make good conversation with your outgoing landlord. Get their requirements in writing and price them. Sometimes it's cheaper to negotiate a cash settlement than to do the work

## 2 months out — tell everyone

- Notify clients and suppliers of the new address and the date
- Update ASIC, your ABN registration, insurance, bank and any licences
- Update your website, email signatures, Google Business Profile and directory listings. The Google Business Profile matters more than people expect for local search
- Order new stationery and business cards
- Confirm building access requirements at both ends — inductions, certificates of currency, after-hours approvals
- Book the end-of-lease clean at the old site and the post-construction clean at the new one. New fit outs produce a remarkable amount of dust, and the builder's clean is not the same as a proper detail clean. [Commercial cleaning](/cleaning) of the outgoing space is part of make good — often required to a higher standard than a normal end-of-lease clean

## 1 month out — logistics

- Confirm dock and lift bookings at both buildings, in writing
- Confirm the IT cutover plan and who is doing it, hour by hour
- Label everything by destination room, not by contents
- Arrange access cards, keys and alarm codes for the new site
- Plan where staff work on move day. Assume nobody is productive in the office that day
- Photograph the old space before you leave. Date-stamped. This is your evidence in any make good dispute
- Confirm final utility readings and disconnection dates

## Move week

- Keys, cards, codes tested before the truck arrives
- One person on site at each end with authority to make decisions
- Test the internet, phones and printers before everyone arrives Monday
- Have the new space cleaned after the furniture is in place, not before
- Keep a defects list from day one. Doors, power points, blinds, air conditioning. Raise them together while the builder is still engaged

## After the move

- Complete make good on the old space and get written sign-off from the outgoing landlord
- Chase your bond or bank guarantee release. This does not happen automatically
- Set each workstation up properly with the person who sits at it. Chair height, monitor height, [desk height](/blog/height-adjustable-desks-newcastle). Twenty minutes per person, once
- Walk the floor at four weeks and ask what isn't working. Small fixes are cheap now and annoying forever if left
- Diarise your next lease expiry and option notice date the week you move in. That's not pessimism — that's the whole point of this checklist

## The five that catch people out

1. The option notice period. Diarise it the day you sign, not the year it's due.
2. Make good. Read it early, price it early, negotiate it early.
3. Fibre lead times. Ordered last, needed first.
4. Furniture ordered too late. It's the last thing bought and the first thing used.
5. Nobody owning the project. A move sits between the landlord, the builder, the IT provider, the furniture supplier and the removalist. When it belongs to everyone it belongs to no one, and the person it lands on is usually the office manager, on top of their actual job.

## Who should be doing this

Someone in your business can absolutely run an office move. Plenty do. It just costs more than it looks like it does — not in fees, but in the weeks of leadership attention that come off revenue work while it's happening.

That's what we do at Your Office Space. We're Newcastle-based, we work for the tenant and never the landlord, and we handle the [lease](/tenant-rep), the [fit out](/furniture), the [furniture](/furniture) and the [ongoing cleaning](/cleaning) as one job with one point of contact.

If you've got a lease expiry coming up in the next eighteen months, the useful conversation is now — not when the notice period is three weeks out.
